title: The point of posts about AI made this game in X hours
author: seahorse-emoji
selftext:
This is a genuine question from a traditional games professional who is very bullish on AI powered game dev.

I wonder what the utility of all these posts going AI made this game in X hours is? Are they demo's of the AI's capabilities ? Are they precursors to promotion for the game ? Or are they just excitement that needs somewhere to go ? (I'm sure it's gotta be impressive to see an AI just make a thing) ? Perhaps they are something else entirely.

I ask because it seems like this sub is drowning in posts about games AI made in X hours. 

For the record, even though I am very in favor of developers using AI for all aspects of making games, I really don't think these fully autonomously made games will stand up to real players or a real marketplace.

I wonder if the time may have come to start asking people to post more about the work they are doing, the cool game they are making, the problems they are having making games; Over "AI made this in X hours"

comments.author: Embarrassed_Text_347
comments.body: I don't think it's the flex people think it is... Building something in a few hours just means that you didn't put very much effort into it. If it's capable of building something good in that amount of time, it could probably do something great if you spent more time on it. I'd rather see those results.

replies.author: seahorse-emoji
replies.body: It's a demo of the AI's capabilities but not much more; and I imagine that most people here think that AI is infact impressively capable

comments.author: j1343
comments.body: People who are serious about AI game dev and spending lots of time on it are not posting their work because there is no benefit in doing so. And if youre trying to make money you absolutely do not want people knowing your game is built with AI.

replies.author: seahorse-emoji
replies.body: The current climate is definitely hostile to AI powered games, that will definitely change though. These things always do. I just wonder when people will actually move on from "Look at what AI can one shot"

replies.author: BlueAndYellowTowels
replies.body:
...and this is the elephant in the room. Right? Normally, in a development sub, you'll see posts about problems for a project. Game or website, doesn't matter. But, AI games, are different in that, people aren't really sharing because the basic truth is if they explain their game... someone can just take it. Because if their AI can make a game, then someone's AI can make the same game and he only way to "protect" your "idea" is to not share it.

Which is terrible for a community and not just that, but the basic truth is competition will be STEEP. Because if your Astra can do it. So can mine. That's the beauty of AI. It only feels like it's amazing because so few are using it now. But once the Gold Rush ends... forget it... everyone and their mom is going to be able to cook up some game and they won't even bother looking at the majority of products built by AI. 

There might be some rare exception where the person wrangled AI to do something really interesting and unique but most of the time it's going to be stuff anyone else could reproduce with the tool. 

I would guess that the future of the most successful AI games will come from people with significant backgrounds or deep passion for either art or literature... people who take art seriously and supplement their vision with AI.  I would be surprised if we ever see an AI Only game, where every single aspect of the game is generated by AI, do well. I doubt that.

replies.author: seahorse-emoji
replies.body:
Thats definitely an interesting conundrum but I have always maintained that ideas are cheap. I mean, I'm sure getting a game idea copied feels horrible to the person who's idea is being copied but in general the copier can copy most things but not you, not your ideas, not your creativity. That shit they dont get.

Now a dedicated copier with a marketing budget can 100% ruin what could have been a great career. Especially as you said, making games, making identical copies etc will become trivial especially for smaller things, if someone can outmarket you they will outsell you.

I just don't think that the "game idea" is as important as non game devs think it is. It's the execution that matters and even though AI can replicated something that looks fairly identical, replicating the feel is very hard.

replies.author: BlueAndYellowTowels
replies.body:
>but not you, not your ideas, not your creativity.

That depends... how much of your "creativity" have you ceded to AI?

I don't think "you" matter as much as you'd like and your ideas can be copied. The real question is: "How creative is my idea / game really?" and we're going to learn very quickly... not very.

Being creative is hard. This is why artists were pissed off when generative AI was stealing their styles... because they spent real time and effort distinguishing themselves from others.

Same exact problem with AI Games. You can just take any idea and make it your own. Just like how it was done with books and art... and music... that's what happens when no one has any regard for human creativity.

No game anyone makes is going to special. Because the basic truth, is like all the stuff used to build LLMs, it will be taken too to improve the model.

replies.author: seahorse-emoji
replies.body: Interesting, I definitely feel that there is more to it than that but hey, look forward to seeing it play out :)

replies.author: daddywookie
replies.body:
I think a valuable commodity in the future will be the harness you build around the AI. Everybody starts in the same place but over time you build up a layer of process, documents, prompts etc that fine tune the way the AI behaves.

I see a lot of posts of people sharing their cool new process or skill. I think they are giving away their most valuable unique selling point as an AI driven developer. Companies talk about developing a moat but we need to start thinking the same as individuals.

What will get interesting is when companies want to hire an AI first game developer. Do they claim any ownership of the harness? Can I use my personal harness for them without handing it over? It is as much part of my value as my ideas and experiences, but it can be taken and duplicated and then I can be discarded.

replies.author: MildlyConcernedMan91
replies.body: Ok so im building an ARPG right now and if I showed you a trailer and told you what it was about, I 100% guarantee you, you couldn't reproduce it within 1 year, with astra. Because the devil is in the details of the math, the balance, the progression. I've been using astra since day 1 a few days ago, and it's an amazing assistant but I have to finetune it to perfection to get me that fine dopamine balance.

replies.author: Nooberling
replies.body:
Only if your game is fundamentally simple. Making a complex game and making it bug-free with AI is a huge undertaking. Ideas are still fairly cheap and good clean implementation still expensive.

AI can just implement **bigger ideas**. Which is very cool but most people don't understand that.

comments.author: CycleMother2006
comments.body:
They're people brand new to the field getting overly excited about the illusion of progress the models tend to provide in a short time. It's like when someone goes to the gym for their first week ever and thinks they've lost 5 pounds of fat and their muscles have bulked up and they are kings of the world. In reality, they lost 10 pounds of water weight and had 1 pounds of glycogen and water shuffle into the muscles that were lying dormant and unused.  And then they probably lost 1 actual pound of fat in all that.

However they think, "At this rate I'm going to be fit in like 4 more weeks?" But in actuality it'll take 40 more weeks to reach that end goal at the true rate, and will only get harder mentally and emotionally as their progress slows to the real rate.

Which is why you don't really see the posts crop up from the same people.

I do think it's interesting when someone actually pushes a prompt to its limits or finds something that a model does surprisingly well. Some of the things I'd dismissed as being impossible for AI had been proven wrong to me here and had me go and tinker further with my own agents until I got it working properly. So it's not all bad. But yes, I do wish we had a separate section for just "vibe benchmarks". That's really all they are. I question how many of the makers are actual gamers or phone gamers, because I feel like the only way you see some of these things and think, "Wow this'll sell like hotcakes!" is if Flappy Bird was your main jam. Not trying to dig on an entire market but... it's oversaturated for a reason.

replies.author: seahorse-emoji
replies.body:
There's definitely some overestimation happening. Not sure how many people see the one shots and feel like they are 4 weeks from ship but I can imagine someone looking at what seemed an impossible target one year ago hit in just few hours.

My own version of this came from AI just autonomously implementing a basic match 3 game.. like I know what that shit takes, and the fact that it did it in an hour is impressive in the extreme.

I'm just looking forward to the time when people get past the "I made a GTA clone using AI"

a. You didnt  
b. What would be the point if you did ? What I wanna see is something fun and unique not GTA clones or Roguelike # 637

replies.author: shlaifu
replies.body: everyone's going for fun and unique, and customers buy their good old favourite genre. - so... uniqueness may not be a desirable for most. Making roguelike #637 with unique graphics probably has better chances in the market then wildly creative game #4

replies.author: seahorse-emoji
replies.body:
possibly, playing to the market is a better way to pay your bills. I've always been more interested in games as art though.

But Balatro is a commercially successful thing that was wildly creative when it came out, I guess I am just hoping for more of that

replies.author: shlaifu
replies.body:
I don't disagree with you in general -but I am struggling with the games-as-art thing. Mainly because: art-reception is very differently, more passively, and in a contemplative mode. Games are interactive, they trigger the player to do and interact. I mean, you would likely get bored and bewildered by an artwork that's 13 hours of disemboweling creatures - but there's a bunch of games which could be well described that way.

anyway, what I'm trying to say is: uniqueness is a valid unique sales proposition, but going for it is a high-risk-high-reward strategy. So what you want to see is developers taking risks.

comments.author: oscar_unrealizex
comments.body:
AI can feel like cheating, especially if 1. someone doesn't disclose it and 2. if others aren't using AI. I don't want to do flame wars, but they come from a place of honesty IMO, even if you disregard the other AI issues. But when anyone can access AI workflows, how to discuss it in a collegiate manner? This is not like a car, where you and I would drive it the same. 2 users with the same monthly budget for AI, and even the same technical background, get VASTLY different results and mileage.   
  
So I think it comes from a place of honesty, in that the best, most accurate way to understand this tech responsibly is open sandbox discussions of workflows. Peoples' daily reports on "I asked for Y and got this result" are the most accurate up-to-date textbook on what you can do.

replies.author: seahorse-emoji
replies.body:

replies.author: kultcher
replies.body:
Yeah, as someone who uses Godot, I find it odd that the Godot community is pretty hostile toward AI. Like I wonder if they realize how many shortcuts modern game programs give you by, y'know, doing all the physics and fancy lighting for you.

There are some Godot nodes that probably have as much underlying code (or at least as much code complexity) as a small game all by themselves, and I'm sure the same can be said for similar structures in Unreal or Unity.

comments.author: CraigBMG
comments.body:
Before AI, I used to see a lot of "make Minecraft in an afternoon!" type videos and posts.  No, they didn't.  They implemented a fairly simple voxel engine.  Minecraft is a complex and finely tuned crafting and survival game with interesting mobs, redstone circuits, multiplayer... list continues.  
  
That is to say, a bunch of this stuff is similar:  surface level, unpolished, and unoriginal.

Now, making this stuff with AI is fun - arguably, the making is the game itself now.  And perhaps that is what people are posting, and I will disparage no one for using these amazing tools to have fun.

comments.author: BlueAndYellowTowels
comments.body:
I don't mean this in any serious way and the way I'm going to frame it, is likely going to be a little harsh.

The majority of "Made x in y hours" posts, are basically, the equivalent of people learning how to use the SUM() function in Excel. It's such low hanging fruit, it's almost laughable. 

I don't make games for a living but I make enterprise software. So, very deeply complex systems and to me, the responses to those posts are kinda funny.

My biggest pet peeve from this sub is this: People who think the coding was the challenge. Who think that all they needed for game development was just a tool to write the code for them... and it's so misguided, it's not even rooted in reality.

Where I work, we use AI extensively in every step of the development process. From User Stories, to Technical and User Requirements. We also use it development and QA. And even if the AI churned out the PERFECT code, it still takes a long time to build things because, you product is only as good as the description of the problem it solves is.

...and with games, that's a very amorphous thing. Most of what we see, is people cloning things that exist already and saying "SEE WHAT'S POSSIBLE!?" and not using the tool to create anything interesting, or engaging or... sellable. 

And that's largely because all the dweebs from back in the day who had their "revolutionary game idea" but couldn't code for shit who kept trying to rope me (and other devs) into their edgelord fantasy game were never creative or driven to begin with and because that remains still true, they think they finally got one over on programmers now that they have AI but they're still lazy, still undisciplined and still have no vision.

They're just people who have a coding bot they can annoy instead of some poor programmer who has to listen to another milquetoast "idea" from a mediocre mind that couldn't be bothered to learn what a variable is.

And now I am taking things slow, 1 step at a time and learn what I can while using AI to polish my game. And personally, I feels like i just dont have enough time, too many things I want to work on my game, cant imagine how people can say "this is done in x hours" lol

comments.author: UncleJoesLandscaping

The issue with this approach is often that a prompt can take you 50% or even further in a very short time, but getting the next 50% will ve 99% of the work.

It takes the 80/20 pareto principle to the extreme. A large bulk of the game can be generated extremely fast, but getting a fully functional fun game is still a lot of work.

comments.author: imnotabot303
comments.body:
It's a similar thing in all AI subs. It's basically a bunch of people who have very little or no knowledge or experience in what they are doing, that get excited when it looks like they can make something by doing almost nothing.

Go to the aivideo sub for example and it's the same thing, people posting endless short clips that are mainly just disposable brain rot content and memes but full of comments on every post about how Hollywood is cooked or how this time next year they are all going to be making full length movies.

It's no different here, people see a half assed tech demo of a game concept one shotted or created in X amount of time and think they will be able to ship a game with a week's worth of work and be rolling in money.

Tbh I think the mods should just ban it, the sub has just turned into one long Astra ad lately.

Unless these kind of posts have an extensive breakdown of what was done, or it's some kind of comparison, they are useless. If you want to just see Astra tech demos there's hundreds of them on YouTube now.

replies.author: seahorse-emoji
replies.body: I am hesitant to give more work to mods, but I do think that the culture on the sub could change to one that rewards real discussions more than. AI adevertising

replies.author: imnotabot303

Yes I think most people joined this sub to get insights and tips on how game devs are using AI in their workflows. Not to see constant spam from non game devs posting their first game idea that was one shotted or took 2 days for AI to make which is probably just a clone of a game that already exists anyway.

Sometimes this sub feels a bit like if a non AI game dev sub just had constant posts from beginners who had just done their first tutorial and posted the results. After a while it starts to get tedious and starts to feel like spam if too many people are doing it.

I don't mind those posts that much if they include useful information but a lot of them don't include anything useful at all or it's just LLM output being included.

comments.author: Neither_Berry_100

These showcases are far from finished playable games. A few unique mechanics or whatever doesn't make a game. Making a good game is very difficult.

And games can be stolen. Not just from AI rebuilding it. I've seen multiple posts about games getting reverse engineered, modified, and sold.

comments.author: fallaxmallum
comments.body:
I see it as a sign that people are testing the waters. AI is giving people who lack coding knowledge and experience the ability to create games in a relatively short amount of time. Some people are testing its capabilities, and others are starting to take notice.

We had trash games before AI, and we're probably going to see an increase in even trashier games because of it. But AI is also going to create opportunities for talented people without coding experience to make genuinely good games that they otherwise might never have been able to create.

Only time will tell.

replies.author: seahorse-emoji
replies.body: Definitely seems plausible, some folks are definitely in the testing waters camp and will hopefully graduate to actually making something worth playing

comments.author: Beskull

comments.author: Entropydemic
comments.body:
What used to take months takes days, and it's very exciting for those of us who spent at much time on a project, to be able to have that time cut away.

For example, when I was developing Age of Conan Hyborean Adventures, we had no less than fifty employees in four countries all working tirelessly over the course of two years, not counting the additional set up time taken to acquire the licenses and publisher beforehand, hiring employees, translators, community setup, government funding (yes, Norway funded over a few million into Age of Conan) and so on. Then... Poor practices, Eidos Interactive pressuring us to compete against what would be World of Warcrafts biggest release, corporate mismanagement from Funcom, and a lot of bad press from employees sexting customers, led to our game being crushed and phased out.

Now we have the power for one person to make their entire vision come to fruition without publisher pressure as well as design working systems within hours or days. That's fuckin' huge.

replies.author: Entropydemic
replies.body: For a little context, World of Warcraft was already the industry leader in all of video game territory at the time. Their upcoming expansion, "Wrath of the Lich King" was announced halfway through our last year of development, and our publisher Eidos Interactive told our community management to announce a release date scheduled before Blizzard releases theirs in an attempt to 'usurp' their customer base. However, us programmers were having a shit time just trying to program the door in the starter town. (Tortage)

Playing it would be akin to reading a book made by the prompt "Write me a great book about a mystery". AI should be the tool, not what makes the game in your stead.

comments.author: Square-Yam-3772
comments.body:
my recent example with Astra:

And then I came across one of the "Astra made this game in X hours" posts that is somewhat close to what I was doing. 

so I adjust my plan because now I learned that Astra can actually do it

comments.author: EC36339
comments.body:
I see a lot of comments here that basically say "game development is supposed to take time. Otherwise the game will be slop", but nobody explaining why.

A few days ago, I spent hours building, editing and fine tuning ONE shader to make ONE enemy in my game look roughly the way I wanted it to look. And I'm still not satisfied.

And I used AI to write 100% of that shader (minus tweaking a few numbers by hand, which is faster and cheaper than telling the AI: "set this variable to 0.6")

Is it because I didn't use the latest model? No. It's because I wanted to build something very specific that I had in mind, and no LLM in the world can do that. AI can vomit out something random that might even look good, but it's not what I want.

And even if you let it produce something random, you may still get garbage among garbage. The stuff we see here that look impressive is the product of publication bias. Hundreds or thousands of people try to make games with single prompts every day. Only the ones that don't look absolute shit get posted.

It's like that scene in an old Simpsons episode where Bart is showing that his dog is well-trained by telling him to go and sniff the butthole of another dog.

I've never seen anyone bragging about how they made any major updates to their one-prompt games. Either AI can't do it, or their "developers" have no interest in it, which is proof that these games aren't good after all, because a game that actually gets people excited would be seeing further development, of only because its one single player, who is also its developer, wants to see new stuff in it. So what happens to these games built with billions of tokens after they get posted here? Do they go straight into the trash?

AI is definitelt helpful, and it helped me build a custom engine and playable vertical slice of a game in only a few months using spec-driven development and affordable models while AFK half of the time. Yes, half, because just testing and fine tuning the stuff that comes iut of AI takes hours, not because the AI is bad, but because it can't see the screen or listen to a sound and read my mind and know that's what I wanted. The difference between "make me somwthing random" and getting precisely the thing you want is days (sometimes hours) vs months.

Am I negative to AI or unimpressed with it? Not at all. I'm in the process of building workflows that actually make AI work the way I want for producing content, with data-driven effects and short feedback loops. I can already make AI mass produce sound effects, then pick the good ones and fine tune them. Doing the same with vfx using the same method is the next step, and I'm already seeing good results. AI can do magic if you give it constraints and basic domain-specific LEGO bricks rather than telling it to build from scratch.

It is also great for discussing game design with, better than most humans.

comments.author: heavy-minium
comments.body:
On social media there are a lot of people that enjoy inciting strong reactions and drawing attention from others. It's part of their dopamine ritual. It's why people report popular stuff although there is little benefit in doing so.

So taking something made by AI that looks impressive is exactly that - they get explosive reactions, dopamine feedback, that makes them addicted to it, they do it more.

Frankly I'm not too worried about too much slop landing on Steam and co. because you still need two ingredients that AI can't give you and most people don't have: perseverance and responsibility.

perseverance -> you need to finish that fucking game, and that means going through gruesome work that you all postponed toward the end of release because you already did everything which is fun to do first.

responsibility -> you need to support that game. There's no "sorry, AI can't find out why it crashes on your hardware". And there's little longevity with most of the people that one-shotted stuff so far because they aren't using any version control system (good luck in attempting to never destroy your project files with AI, lol).

What's going to happen instead is that you will have people addicted to the satisfying dopamine loop of quickly putting something together with AI and then moving on to the next thing before realizing any value from what they did.

comments.author: Kim_Laone
comments.body: I've been working on one of my games (a construction puzzle game on a phaser) since November (7-8 months, because I took breaks) and it's probably 40-60% ready. However, my attempt to put it on the itchio failed, and technical support hasn't responded yet and my page is still hanging in a draft closed state. That's why I haven't written anything about the game yet... I hope this problem will be solved and I'll finish the game to the end. I've been working on the second game for about 2 months - but it's probably 5-10%. This game is a kind of symbiosis of an RPG and a simulator on the Godot engine. The game mechanics there are based on several mini-games and they all work alone with test sprites-stubs. However, these mini-games still need to be harmoniously combined in the form of quests, interaction with the world at least at the level of several quests for such a complete vertical slice of the game.  So the plans are to bring the prototype to at least 20-25% with the opportunity to show it and then refine it. But the failure with the first game makes me doubt myself and makes my mood swing like waves from "everything is bad, life is shit" to "everything is fine, I can do anything")... Of course, I will still try to implement my ideas with the help of AI (code, localization, partial drawing, all kinds of help and tips on how and where to find this or that information, and so on) - because I like doing this. However, it would be interesting to hear feedback from people about my game (what was incomprehensible, interesting, boring, etc.).
